processing_steps_notes.value: Alloys were made of high-purity elements (Fe, Mn, Al, C and Be, 99.99%) and melted into alloy ingots in a vacuum induction melting furnace under a high-purity argon atmosphere. The obtained ingot has a diameter of 60 mm and a thickness of 30 mm. This is the terminal as-cast state: the as-cast Fe–Mn–Al–C steel was not given any heat treatment or thermal deformation, so no uniform microstructure is obtained.

interface_notes.value: In the as-cast 0.5Be steel the atomic concentration ratio of Fe to Be atoms is 18.7:1; the Be–Fe phase (beryllium compound) is randomly distributed and attached to the austenite matrix. The formation of the Be–Fe phase is reported to be observed when the mass percentage of Be to Fe reaches 1:4 in a certain region, and the Be–Fe phase precipitates at the boundary between austenite and ferrite in the as-cast structure of the higher-Be steels. The Be–Fe phase in the as-cast 0.5Be steel cannot be tested by microhardness (instrument limitation).

phase_evolution.value: With increasing Be content the as-cast structure changes from a single austenite (0Be, 0.5Be) to a γ + δ dual-phase structure (1.0Be, 1.5Be): the addition of Be promotes the formation of the ferrite phase. For the 0.5Be alloy, beryllium first forms Be–Fe compounds (Be11Fe and Be12Fe) rather than ferrite — no ferrite was observed by XRD when 0.5Be was added to the Fe–30Mn–10Al–1.5C matrix, whereas at 1.0 wt% Be ferrite appears. For Be, compounds are likely formed first, before ferrite structures.

overall_structure.value: As-cast 0.5Be steel is composed of a single austenite (γ) matrix plus a small amount of Be–Fe compound precipitates (Be11Fe and Be12Fe); no ferrite was detected by XRD. The matrix shows a cellular/dendritic solidification structure whose cell boundaries are decorated with dark, point-like beryllium compound particles. Be addition produces rod-like, needle-like and Chinese-character shaped compounds in the as-cast microstructure.
